title: UEFA and CONCACAF Challenge FIFA: Give $2.1 Billion to Member Nations
summary:
Two of FIFA's vice presidents are challenging world soccer's governing body over its money. UEFA President Aleksander Ceferin and CONCACAF President Victor Montagliani sent a letter Friday to FIFA President Gianni Infantino calling for an independent review of FIFA's financial reserves and proposing a $2.1 billion payout to all 211 member associations.

The proposal would make at least $10 million available to each member association over the 2027-30 cycle, on top of funding already committed under FIFA's Forward Programme. The money would go toward infrastructure and football development.

The tension traces back to the abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise project. FFE had been presented to member associations as a plan to sell an interest in FIFA's competitions to outside investors to generate more money for development. It was dropped after a backlash. But Ceferin and Montagliani say their analysis of FIFA's published financial statements raises a question: was that transaction even necessary? They say FIFA is on course to end the 2023-26 cycle with reserves of about $6 billion — the largest in its history — and already has the capacity to distribute substantially more from its own balance sheet.

"Our analysis now raises an important question as to whether the proposed transaction was necessary to deliver greater resources to the MAs," the letter said. Even after the payout, they argue, FIFA's reserves would not fall below about $1.5 billion at any point in the next cycle — roughly 50 percent above the minimum reserve level FIFA itself budgeted for 2023-26.

They acknowledged their analysis was preliminary, combining published results for 2022-25 with estimates for 2026 and assumptions for 2027-30, and called for an independent review with full access to the figures. The letter also frames the issue as one of governance: "Development is an institutional responsibility of FIFA — not a matter of individual discretion." Ceferin and Montagliani said they would ask the other four continental confederation presidents to support the proposal. FIFA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
why_it_matters: Money in global sports decides which countries can build pitches, train coaches, and give kids a chance to play, so a fight over billions at FIFA is really a fight over who gets to shape the game's future.

background_read: FIFA (the Federation Internationale de Football Association, founded in 1904) is soccer's worldwide governing body and has 211 member associations, one for each country or territory. Gianni Infantino has been FIFA's president since 2016, and Aleksander Ceferin and Victor Montagliani are two of his vice presidents, leading UEFA and CONCACAF respectively.

UEFA (the Union of European Football Associations) runs European competitions such as the Champions League and the European Championship, while CONCACAF (the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football) covers North and Central America and the Caribbean and organizes events like the Gold Cup. Six continental confederations sit under FIFA, which is why the letter's authors plan to ask the other four presidents to back their proposal.

FIFA's reputation for money problems is long: in 2015, U.S. prosecutors charged dozens of soccer officials with corruption, and the organization later promised to push more money toward development through its Forward Programme, the scheme that funds member associations.

The abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise project would have sold an interest in FIFA's competitions to outside investors to raise extra development money, but it was dropped after member associations objected. Ceferin and Montagliani now argue that FIFA's own reserves show the sale was never necessary.

perspectives.description: A $2.1 billion payout would send at least $10 million to every member association, including small nations that struggle to fund basic facilities. Supporters say the money already exists and should be shared rather than hoarded, and that outside investors were never needed.

FIFA has not publicly responded, and critics of the proposal note that the analysis is preliminary, blending published figures with estimates and assumptions. Some officials may worry that draining reserves leaves FIFA exposed if a World Cup or broadcast deal falls through, or that a one-time payout does not fix long-term governance problems.

FIFA's 2015 corruption scandal showed how opaque its money once was, and the Forward Programme was partly a response to that. Seen this way, the letter is the latest round in a decades-long tug-of-war between FIFA's central leadership and the continental confederations over who controls the game's wealth.

The real question may be structural: if reserves are as healthy as the letter claims, why did FIFA consider selling a stake in its competitions at all? An independent review with full access to the figures would either settle the argument or expose how little members know about the body that runs their sport.
